newsitem.title: USA: Coffee soars as speculators buy, gold eases on Fed move.
newsitem.headline: Coffee soars as speculators buy, gold eases on Fed move.

text.p: Coffee futures soared on Tuesday on speculative buying as professional traders found little selling interest from Latin American producers and pushed the market to its sharpest gain in a week.
In other markets, grain prices rose on crop worries and precious metals closed lower after the Federal Reserve nudged up interest rates for the first time in two years.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for delivery in May closed 16.40 cents a pound higher at 179.30 cents.
Latin American producers appeared to have moved to the sidelines ahead of the long Easter weekend after selling futures and stepping up shipments in recent weeks.
"What we saw was a technically inspired rally with origin activity on the slack side," said Prudential Securities analyst Arthur Stevenson.
"There was nothing behind today's move," said Stephen Smith, president of South Futures in Miami. "More than anything, the market proved to itself that it reached a bottom -- and away we went."

May coffee hit a high of 209.50 cents on March 5, up from a low of 102.60 cents on December 6, driven by tight supplies at roasters, strikes in number two producer Colombia, and doubts about the size of this year's crop in Brazil.

Coffee producers used the soaring prices to step up shipments. But despite a steady recovery of consumer stocks in recent weeks, which eased supply concerns, analysts said tight coffee supplies looked to be a long-term factor this year.
"There is a realization that we had some coffee coming in and now it's going to slow down," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "The producers are well sold."
Precious metals in New York ended lower after the Federal Reserve tightened credit for the first time in two years, raising the Federal funds rate a quarter point to 5.5 percent.

"The interest rate factor, although discounted and talked about, is certainly not bullish," William O'Neill of Merrill Lynch said. "Rate hikes in the current non-overly inflationary atmosphere are just not psychologically good, and there is an opportunity lost with higher interest rates for metals."
June gold at the Commodity Exchange ended $2.50 lower at $350.50 an ounce and May silver 7.70 cents lower at $5.12.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean futures rose on news of a fire at the key Brazilian port of Paranagua. That fed concern that soybean exports from Brazil would slow and U.S. exports would receive a boost.
May soybeans ended 10-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $8.42.
"I think this rally was more about value than the fire," said Mickey Luth, analyst with the Laifa Group in Chicago.
"Monday's losses were overdone, particularly going into a report that could be bullish," Luth said.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture next Monday will release its first estimate of 1997 soybean plantings based on farmer surveys, with traders expecting 65.5 to 66.5 million acres, up from last year's 64.2 million.
Wheat prices also rose after weekly crop condition reports on Monday indicated dryness was posing a threat to the young winter wheat crop in Texas and Oklahoma.
May wheat rose 3 cents a bushel to close at $3.89-1/2.

Last week's news that Taiwan was suspending its pork exports also continued to have effects on corn and hog markets. Corn prices rose on expectations that the U.S. hog herd would expand and feed demand rise to replace Taiwan exports.
May corn rose 3-1/4 cents a bushel to $3.02-1/4.
"The instant improvement in the hog feeding margins has created a lot of pricing," said E.D. and F. Man International analyst Charlie Sernatinger.
At the Chicago Mercantile Exchange, June hogs closed 1.30 cents a pound lower at 80.85 cents on profit-taking after three straight days of limit gains totaling 6 cents.
"It's a little bit of correction against the trend," said Dennis Smith, broker with LIT division of First Options.
On the New York Mercantile Exchange, heating oil rose as cold weather on the East Coast appeared to take traders by surprise. April heating oil closed up 1.10 cents a gallon at 56.83 cents.

May crude oil closed down 7 cents a barrel at $20.99 and Aoirl unleaded gasoline ended up 0.01 cent a gallon at 66.52 cents, with both markets awaiting weekly petroleum stocks data from the American Petroleum Institute after the close.
